blocks.text: Another name of the locust, ἀττάκης [attakēs] or ἀττακὸς [attakos] in Levit. XI, 22., might seem [col. 449] also to take its name from ἄττειν [attein], from leaping, as in the vulgar tongue saltarella. Unless ἀττακὸς [attakos] is thought to be the same as ἀστακὸς [astakos] in the dialect of the Aeolians, for whom πίστις [pistis] is πίττις [pittis], whence fides [faith]; and βλάστη [blastē] is βλάττη [blattē], whence planta [plant]. In favour of this are: 1. that among the sea locusts there is the ἀστακὸς [astakos], astacus (in Norman houmar); 2. that in the best Glosses lucusta, or locusta, is rendered ἀκρὶς [akris], ἀστακός [astakos]. Nor do these words of Isidore, otherwise very inept, mean anything else: "The locust is so called because it has long legs like a spear [hasta]; hence the Greeks call it, both the marine and the terrestrial kind, hastago." For it is evident that he was reaching after frigid wordplays between locusta, hasta and astacus, as though the astacus, his hastago, were a kind of terrestrial as well as of marine locust.

There is also in Levit. XI, 22. a species of locust called ὀφιομάχης [ophiomachēs], ophiomachus, as if it fought serpents. However παράδοξον [paradoxon] this is, the Philosopher nevertheless affirms it in the History [III, 264], book 9, chapter 6: Πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ τὴν ἀκρίδα ἑωράκασιν, ὅτι ὅταν μάχηται τοῖς ὄφεσι, λαμβάνεται τοῦ τραχήλου τῶν ὄφεων [Polloi de kai tēn akrida heōrakasin, hoti hotan machētai tois ophesi, lambanetai tou trachēlou tōn opheōn]. Hence Pliny, book 11, chapter 29: "Each one by itself kills a serpent, when it pleases, seizing its throat with its bite." And Simon Majolus, bishop of Volturara, in Dialogue 10, relates that his gardener, coming from the field, saw a locust that had seized a serpent by the throat and so killed it without a fight. It should be noted that ὀφιομάχης [ophiomachēs] is put in the Law for the Hebrew חרגל chargol, or argol. For by the usage of the ancients it can be written either way. Thus the same river of Mesopotamia, חבר, is written in Greek Χαβόρας [Chaboras] and Ἀβόρας [Aboras]. The same people of Arabia Felix, חצרמות, Χατραμῶται [Chatramōtai] and Ἀτραμῶται [Atramōtai]. And among the Leuco-Syrians the Alybes are the same as the Chalybes. And the חסידים are called now Chasidaei, now Asidaei. And the bird חסידה chasida is written ἄσιδα [asida] in the Greek version of Job. So I think that the ancients wrote the Hebrew name of the ophiomachus, חרגול chargol, as argol, with the aspiration dropped. And from this arose the fable of the argolae ophiomachi, which they idly claim were serpents rather than locusts, and were called argolae because they were brought by Alexander from Pelasgian Argos into Egypt to kill the asps. So Suidas reports: Ἀργόλαι· εἶδος ὄφεων, οὓς ἤνεγκε Μακεδὼν ὁ Ἀλέξανδρος ἐκ τοῦ Ἄργους τοῦ Πελασγικοῦ εἰς Ἀλεξάνδρειαν, καὶ ἐνέβαλεν εἰς τὸν ποταμὸν, πρὸς ἀναίρεσιν τῶν ἀσπίδων [Argolai; eidos opheōn, hous ēnenke Makedōn ho Alexandros ek tou Argous tou Pelasgikou eis Alexandreian, kai enebalen eis ton potamon, pros anairesin tōn aspidōn]. Nor does he cite an authority. But I find something similar in the Synopsis on the Life and Death of the Prophets, which they falsely ascribe to Dorotheus the martyr, in the chapter On Jeremiah. But instead of a locust ophiomachus there was in Argos a locust scorpiomachus, of which the Philosopher says this in the book of Marvels [ch. 151.]: Ἐν Ἄργει δέ φασι γίνεσθαι ἀκρίδος τινὸς γένος, ὃ καλεῖται σκορπιομάχον· ὅταν γὰρ ἴδῃ τάχιστα σκορπίον, ἀνθίσταται αὐτῷ, ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ ὁ σκορπίος ἐκείνῃ [En Argei de phasi ginesthai akridos tinos genos, ho kaleitai skorpiomachon; hotan gar idē tachista skorpion, anthistatai autō, hōsautōs de kai ho skorpios ekeinē]: "In Argos they say there is a kind of locust, called scorpiomachus, which, as soon as it sees a scorpion, rises against it, as the scorpion in turn against it" ^{(20)}. See the rest there, and in Stobaeus, chapter 98, which is On Diseases, where he cites these very words, though not from Aristotle but from Trophilus.

Ἀκρὶς [Akris] too, the name common to all locusts, is taken in the same passage of Leviticus for a particular species. Because κὰρ [kar] or κάρη [karē] is head, some think it is called ἀκρὶς [akris] as if ἀκαρὶς [akaris], either from a small or from a large head, according as the prefixed Alpha has privative or intensive force. Others derive it παρὰ τὸ ἄκρας τῶν ἀσταχύων καὶ τῶν φυτῶν νέμεσθαι [para to akras tōn astachyōn kai tōn phytōn nemesthai]. So the Etymologicum. But for Eustathius ἀκρὶς [akris] is as if ἀγρὶς [agris], from γράω [graō], that is, ἐσθίω [esthiō]. Since these are rather far-fetched, it seems more probable to me [III, 265] that ἡ ἀκρίς [hē akris] is named ὀνοματοποιητικῶς [onomatopoiētikōs] from its chirping. In its fight with the scorpion the locust κύκλῳ περιϊοῦσα τρύζει περὶ αὐτὸν [kyklō periiousa tryzei peri auton], "going round about it, chirps around it." So the Philosopher has it in the passage just cited.
